turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Saturday, the third of October. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go.
Seven governments opened their oil reserves yesterday, and the price of oil went up.
[laughs] That's not a typo, is it. And a hobby desk where the punchline is that nobody in this country has flown a serious kite since March.
[wry] We have the data on that one. We went and got it ourselves.
Plus a country that counted its own people and found eight hundred thousand more than it thought it had. Nobody moved.
Start with the oil, because it's the cleanest example of something this whole issue is about. Push a system, and it doesn't always move the way you pushed it.

So. The G seven — that's the United States, Canada, Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, plus the European Union — agreed yesterday to release one hundred million barrels through the International Energy Agency, over four months. Starting immediately, and front-loaded on diesel. Diesel in the first twenty days. Because diesel is the actual shortage. Crude is tight. Diesel is the thing that's broken. American on-highway diesel averaged six dollars thirty-eight a gallon in the week to the twenty-eighth of September. European diesel has hit two euros twenty-four a litre, against one fifty-nine before the war started in February.
[exhales] That's a freight problem, a farming problem and a heating problem all at once.
All three. And what triggered it was a threat — Washington had floated banning American diesel exports. Europe said no. An overnight call between Macron and Trump closed the gap.
Analysts put a number on what that ban would have done, didn't they?
Forty to fifty per cent on European wholesale prices. That's the number the statement was written to avoid.
Okay. So the reserves open. And then?
[deadpan] Brent crude went up zero point four per cent. Up. And West Texas Intermediate — the American barrel — fell one point seven eight per cent. Same session.
Wait — so the two big oil benchmarks moved in opposite directions on the same news.

[thoughtful] Eleven dollars forty-eight apart at the close. And that gap is the market telling you something quite precise. The release lands in the Atlantic basin. The risk premium lives east of the Strait of Hormuz. So the market marked down the barrel the reserves can reach, and marked up the one they can't.
[thoughtful] The intervention worked on the wrong ocean. What's the honest scale of a hundred million barrels?
Spread evenly, about eight hundred and thirty thousand barrels a day. Global demand is roughly a hundred and three million a day. So under one per cent.
And against the Gulf?
Kpler put sixteen and a half million barrels a day leaving the Middle East in September — close to pre-war. The entire release is about six days of that outflow. Six days.
Did anyone defend it?

One primary document did, and I like it precisely because it's not from a bank. The Bank of Japan's Summary of Opinions, published Thursday, notes that feared damage to economic activity has — their words — not materialised, partly due to the use of petroleum reserves.
So reserves have worked once already.
Once already. Goldman Sachs is relayed as putting the effect at around half the recent price rise — but I want to flag that we're quoting that second-hand. We didn't read the note.
Good. And one thing I loved in the issue — the viewpoint panels.

Four outlets, four completely different stories about one document. Al Jazeera files it as Trump's trophy. Euronews files it as European capitulation, and is the only one that leads with the engineering problem — crude releases don't automatically become diesel, refineries have to process the oil. Xinhua's English index converted a hundred million barrels of oil and products into a hundred million barrels of diesel. Which isn't what the statement says. [deadpan] Ran nothing. No release, no Hormuz, no carrier. Friday's lead items were Golden Week tourism, a fighter jet sale, and pandas. We print the absence. It's data.
Right, the money block. And I want to start with the jobs number, because it broke a rule.
American payrolls for September came in at twenty-nine thousand. Consensus was somewhere around ninety to a hundred thousand.
So a miss of about sixty thousand. That's a big miss.
Unemployment four point two per cent. The prior two months revised down.
Normally — and correct me — a weak jobs number is good news for bonds. Growth looks shaky, rates come down, bond prices go up.
Normally, yes. That is the reflex of the last two decades. The two-year yield rose five basis points. The ten-year rose four. The thirty-year rose two.
[pause] Everything sold off. On a weak number.

[pause] Everything sold off on a weak number. Bad news has stopped being good news for duration. Because this inflation is a cost shock, not a demand boom. The Federal Reserve raised rates twelve votes to nil on the sixteenth of September — its first increase in three years — and it's being driven by energy, not by an overheating economy. So a growth miss no longer buys you a bond rally.
Is there a number that proves it's a cost shock rather than an inflation-expectations problem?

There is, and it's my favourite number in the issue. The ten-year breakeven — which is the market's own forecast of inflation — is two point three six per cent. Actual headline inflation is three point four.
So the market is pricing inflation lower than it currently is.
Which means the entire rise in yields is real rates and term premium. Not inflation expectations.
[curious] And that explains gold.
That explains gold completely. The ten-year real yield went from two point six two on the twenty-first of September to two point nine two on Friday. Thirty basis points in nine sessions.
And gold did what?
Fell seven point four per cent on the month. While Brent rose seven point four.
So oil up, gold down, in the same month.
Gold isn't failing as an inflation hedge. It's being discounted as a zero-coupon asset while real rates climb. Different mechanism entirely.
What about the equity and bond relationship? The thing that's supposed to protect a balanced portfolio.
[deadpan] It stopped working. Over nine sessions, a global all-world equity fund fell zero point eight six per cent. A global bond fund fell zero point six nine.
Both legs down together.

Positive correlation. That's the signature of a cost shock, and it is the diversification cost of this regime. Not behaving as the liquidity proxy either. Up zero point seven seven per cent on the week — roughly flat while everything else moved — and about a third below its October twenty-twenty-five high, with the Fed tightening.
Who's the dissenter this week?
Mark Zandi at Moody's Analytics, on American public radio Friday. His line: the thing that makes me most nervous is wage growth. People's after-inflation wages are falling.
That's the real economy talking, not the bond market.
And he names the cause directly — the proximate cause is the Iran war. The ten-year was below four per cent, and we haven't looked back.
Anything from inside the Fed?

Governor Michael Barr, on the twenty-ninth: I count only two months of data consistent with two per cent core inflation over the past twenty months. And one that got dated within twenty-four hours. Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said on the first of October that the labour market had stabilised, with unemployment at four point one per cent — near maximum employment.
And the next morning?
It printed four point two.
[chuckles] The data has no manners.
None whatsoever. And this is explanation, not investment advice — the desk says so and so do we.
Singapore. And there's a correction, which I always think is the best thing a magazine prints.

Two corrections. The first is ours. Number one hundred and twenty reported that the haze had broken on Wednesday. [sighs] It had not. At five o'clock this morning the twenty-four-hour index read ninety-five in the Central region. One point below Unhealthy, on the morning the issue went out.
So what happened Wednesday?
A dip. We printed the dip as the end of it. Tuesday the twenty-ninth was the peak — all five regions Unhealthy, Central at a hundred and fifty-five at seven in the morning.
[sighs] And it's still out there.
The haze service's own Friday evening update still describes moderate to dense smoke haze over Singapore, Sumatra and southern Peninsular Malaysia, with dry weather forecast to continue.
What's the good news?
Genuinely good, and it's personal for any parent of a secondary-one girl. From the first of January, the nine-valent HPV vaccine joins the national schedule for females aged nine to twenty-six.
What's the difference against what's used now?
Both cover types sixteen and eighteen — that's seventy per cent of cervical cancers. The nine-valent adds types covering a further twenty. So roughly ninety per cent against seventy.
And the school programme?

This is the detail. Girls in this year's secondary-one cohort who had the bivalent vaccine as their first dose will receive the nine-valent as their second, next year. A mixed schedule the authorities state is safe.
[warmly] So they get the upgrade mid-course. Free, in school, no action required.
No action required. Privately the gap is not small — one clinic lists two hundred and fifty dollars a dose against ninety-six.
And the household bill?
Electricity fell. The quarterly tariff from the first of October is twenty-eight point five nine cents a kilowatt-hour before tax, down from thirty-one ninety-one. A fall of ten point four per cent.
Which, for the record, is the opposite of what this magazine predicted.
[deadpan] We'll get to that. It's on the Scoreboard.

Technology, and this one is genuinely strange. An executive order signed on the twenty-ninth of September abolishes the term artificial intelligence across the American executive branch. The branch shall use the terms Super Intelligence and S I in place of Artificial Intelligence and A I — and will not acknowledge the usage of the old terms in any applicable setting. And for its definition it reaches back to the existing statutory definition — of artificial intelligence.
So the new word is anchored to the old word it refuses to acknowledge. What's the money in it?
[deadpan] There is none. No appropriation. No compute target. No permitting or transmission provision — in the year electricity became the binding constraint on American inference.
How did the technical world take it?
The trade write-up went to Hacker News on the night of signing and finished with eleven points and eight comments. For a presidential action on the defining technology of the decade.
What about real silicon?
One lovely oddity. A chip company amended its agreement to buy another on the first of October — and the price went down nineteen per cent, to about five point seven billion dollars.
Down? After a competing bid appeared?
The filing says plainly that the amendment follows an unsolicited competing proposal from a third party. Unnamed.
So whatever the rival offered, it wasn't more cash.
That's the only reading that works.
And the home lab?

Speculative decoding landed in llama dot cpp on the first. One and a half times faster decoding — one point five five, across twenty-four runs. On exactly one stranger's machine. Three cards, about fifty tokens a second, and he had to cut the micro-batch to load the weights at long context. Someone else hit a loading failure that cleared only when the files were rebuilt.
So: real, fast, and barely tested.
And my favourite line of the week is a code reviewer's, on a different patch. Quote: I test this PR, got crash on one PC, and it's passed on another PC. I think it's no a problem.
[laughs] Was it merged?
It was approved and merged.
[laughs] Beautiful.
The Atelier. Rice cookers. And I want the headline number first.

The grail premium in this category buys you five degrees Celsius. Pressure seals the lid and lifts the boiling point. The makers' own pages give it: one point two atmospheres, a hundred and five degrees, against a hundred.
And where does the money actually go?

[curious] The pot. Tiger's three-layer is one and a half millimetres. Zojirushi's spherical, one point seven. Toshiba's charcoal-coated, two. Hitachi's — which is actual iron, not a coating — two point three.
And the top?
Mitsubishi's is ten millimetres of ninety-nine point nine per cent pure carbon, machined. And it refuses to use pressure on purpose, for a crisp, discrete grain.
[curious] Does the expensive one actually win?
America's Test Kitchen cooked fifty batches across three grain types. The winner was a fuzzy-logic machine at two hundred and forty-three dollars.
Not the flagship?

The induction machine at three hundred produced, their words, softer and wetter rice than desired — for such a large price tag, we expect more consistent results. And the two-hundred-dollar pressure cooker consistently overcooked long-grain rice.
[skeptical] That's a brutal result for the category.
With an honest limit: that's a United States test on American grain. Nobody has blind-tested a Japanese domestic pressure flagship on koshihikari.
And the clay?

Here's the fact I'd repeat at dinner. Eighty to ninety per cent of every earthenware cooking pot made in Japan comes out of one city — Yokkaichi — in a patented clay that's about forty per cent petalite.
So the design brand's donabe is —
A Yokkaichi pot with a logo, quite often.
And the real one?

Nagatani-en, in Iga, founded eighteen thirty-two. Their Kamado-san is two hundred and twenty US dollars. In a category whose electric grail runs to a hundred and thirty-three thousand yen, the clay grail costs under three hundred dollars.
[warmly] I love that.
And a warning for anyone in a condominium: if your hob is induction only, the donabe is out. The maker says so itself — and says even its own induction donabe should not be used to cook rice.
Right — take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole. Kites! And I did not expect to care.

Four crafts share the word and almost nothing else. Single-line, where the craft is in the object. Dual-line, which is the trick vocabulary. Quad-line, which is the one that changes category. [excited] A quad flies backwards. Stops dead. Hovers upside down. It's a machine with a throttle and a reverse gear, not a tethered wing.
And people fall in love how?
Not through a purchase. Through an hour. One newcomer wrote: I spent an hour playing around the edge of a wind column and was hooked.
[thoughtful] The edge of a wind column. You can't see it.
That's the hook. Control at the edge of a physical envelope you cannot see.
Now — the business story, which I did not see coming.

The company that invented quad flying held the patents. They expired. And two workshops took the category. A Chinese factory undercutting it by about half, and one American with a sewing machine and a six-to-eight-week queue. [warmly] An atelier. Custom colours plus fifty dollars, subject to design review, and he signs every kite. A six-model wind ladder from four hundred and ten to four hundred and fifty dollars — the same airframe, six times, with a heavier spar at each step up the wind range.
And what do owners say about the cheap disruptor?

A long-time owner of both: the construction quality of the Freileins I have is probably a step above that of my Revolutions, in terms of uniformity and detail. A year in — no busted spar, no stitch undone, nothing fallen off.
[gasps] That's the incumbent being beaten on build quality.
By the budget brand.
Okay — the Singapore part. This is where the desk did something I really admire.

Rather than quote the published climatology, the desk downloaded every available month of daily records from the Marina Barrage weather station and computed the thing a flier actually needs. The share of days whose daily mean wind reached twelve kilometres an hour. January this year, fifty-eight per cent. February, thirty-two. March, ten.
And the rest?
[pause] April through October, across both years — zero. Not one day.
[drawn out] Not one day.

Singapore isn't windless. It's gusty on top of near-dead air. Daily maxima run twenty-five to thirty-seven kilometres an hour. But sustained, kite-shaped wind only exists from about mid-December to mid-March.
So the global market's standard kites are —
Furniture here, for seven months. The honest local kit is ultralight first, standard second, vented essentially never.
And we're publishing today, which is —
The bottom of the trough. Ten weeks from the good stuff.
[laughs] A hobby desk that tells you not to buy yet.
It tells you to buy the light-wind kite, and learn in dead air.
And the sceptic?

This is the sad part. The gear is thriving and the institutions are dying. A maker warned in February nineteen ninety-nine that as the market shrinks we lose manufacturers, which means fewer new designs and slower innovation.
Did it happen?

You can check his homework by typing web addresses. The canonical American kitemaking supply house now redirects to an unrelated domain. The flagship magazine's last article is dated the eighth of September, twenty fifteen. The competition rulebook hasn't changed since April twenty seventeen.
[sighs] And the forums?

Last week the liveliest corner was people selling nineteen eighty-two kites found unopened in arrow boxes. While the actual growth is on a subreddit full of LED night kites that passes through none of those institutions at all.
Culture and the body, quickly.

A seven-year-old film took the box office in three countries at once. The Endgame re-release. Twenty-six point one million dollars across the United States in three days. Eleven point three million in Japan — in two.
[gasps] Two days in Japan nearly matched three days in America.
Japan didn't see it the way America did the first time. It's less nostalgia there than a delayed first run. It took Singapore too.
And the new releases?

The Tom Cruise film settled at fifty per cent on two hundred and twelve critics — we'd printed fifty-four on a partial count, so the number came back down. A trial we couldn't read last month finally published. A hundred adults, lower-body isometric training three times a week for four weeks: systolic blood pressure down nine point four five millimetres of mercury.
That's a real effect.
And then the useful half. They cut people to three, two, one or zero sessions a week. One session a week keeps most of it. Zero loses all of it inside four weeks.
[thoughtful] So the maintenance dose is one.
One. With the honest caveat that five arms off a hundred people is about twenty per arm, and nobody in it was hypertensive.
And the sceptic?

A Stanford neurologist on the biological-age testing industry: right now, it's a bit like the wild West. And — there are all these companies advertising tests, often with some kind of powder they want to sell you that's never been tested in humans in a clinical trial.
[laughs] There's always a powder.
General information, not medical advice.
The Scoreboard. It's Saturday, so we grade ourselves.
[wry] Eighty-one claims came due. Fifty-five right, twenty-three wrong, two unresolvable.
Start with the worst.
We said Singapore's fourth-quarter electricity tariff would rise toward a modelled twenty to twenty-five per cent range. It fell ten point four per cent.
Direction and magnitude.
[deadpan] Both wrong. And it was our own model, which makes it worse. Three separate issues said the Fed would not hike in September. One said it would. It did, twelve votes to nil.
So the minority view was right.

Three wrong, one right, and the one right was the contrarian. We said Spider-Man would pass two point three billion and not reach two point five. It finished at two billion, four hundred and ninety-seven million, and change.
[laughs] Three million short. That's one good weekend in Italy.

And one pattern worth admitting. Every row where we predicted that no Western newspaper would pick up one of our Undercurrent subjects — we won. Both rows where we predicted a feature would follow — we lost.
So you're good at spotting what the majors ignore —
And bad at guessing when they'll stop ignoring it.
And the long read. Uzbekistan.

[thoughtful] This one stayed with me. On the thirtieth of June, Uzbekistan published the result of its first census since nineteen eighty-nine. Thirty-nine million, forty-seven thousand, three hundred and twenty-one people.
And that was more than expected?
Eight hundred and ten thousand, six hundred and seventeen more than the running official estimate. Two point one per cent, discovered in a morning.
Where were they?
About six hundred thousand of them in one region — the one wrapped around the capital.
[pause] Did they move there?
[pause] Nobody moved. They'd been living there for years.
Then what changed?
Three months before the enumerators arrived, Uzbekistan abolished the propiska — the Soviet residency permit. It had kept it for thirty-four years after the Soviet Union stopped existing.
And under it?

Permanent registration in the capital was restricted to twelve categories of citizen. Everyone else lived and worked there unregistered — which meant without the school place, the clinic, the formal wage.
So admitting where you lived was punishable.
And so the state couldn't see them. Statistical invisibility wasn't a measurement failure. It was a policy output, working exactly as designed, until the design was repealed.
[thoughtful] That's a hell of a sentence.

And the sequence that follows is the argument. Abolish the permit. Count the people. Restrict cash settlement. And from the fifteenth of October — twelve days from now — count every business in the country.
What are they looking for?
Twenty-three per cent of the economy is formally classified as unobserved. Sixty per cent of agricultural turnover. Forty-two per cent of employed people have undocumented income.
So visibility is being offered as a gift.
And will arrive as a bill. The eight hundred thousand who appeared in the ledger this year are the same eight hundred thousand who appear in the tax base next year.
Is that cynical?

I don't think so. The liberations are real — registration is what makes a clinic and a school place available. But a legible state is irreversible. Uzbekistan is building, in eighteen months, exactly the dataset any future and less liberal government would need.
[drawn out] And the register doesn't know what it'll be used for.
[thoughtful] It never does. That's its nature, and it's why every generation has to re-argue who may read it.
What's the line to take away?
Uzbekistan didn't discover eight hundred thousand citizens this year. It stopped making them hide. That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-eight pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
